section.title: The Obedient Servant
section.sectionRationale: This is the third of Isaiah's Servant Songs, and it turns a corner. Israel is confronted with a hard truth, she was not abandoned, she sold herself into exile through her own sin. Against that failure stands the Servant, whose ear is open, whose face is set like flint, and who is struck and spat upon yet never turns back. It is the quiet hinge before the fourth Song, the summit of Isaiah 52:13 to 53:12.
section.thesis: Israel's exile was self-inflicted, not evidence of a failed or forgetful God; and where Israel failed to listen, the Servant listens perfectly, offering His back to those who strike Him rather than turning away, so that His obedience becomes the ground of the salvation Israel could never earn.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the divorce that never happened; the Servant's open ear; the Servant vindicated though shamed; and a closing call to trust the LORD rather than one's own firebrands.

units.label: The divorce that never happened
units.note: Israel sold herself; God did not abandon her

verses.text: This is what the LORD says: “Where is your mother’s certificate of divorce with which I sent her away? Or to which of My creditors did I sell you? Look, you were sold for your iniquities, and for your transgressions your mother was sent away.

Why was no one there when I arrived? Why did no one answer when I called? Is My hand too short to {{gaal|redeem}} you? Or do I lack the strength to deliver you? Behold, My rebuke dries up the sea; I turn the rivers into a desert; the fish rot for lack of water and die of thirst.
I clothe the heavens in black and make sackcloth their covering.”
The Lord GOD has given Me the tongue of {{limmud|discipleship}}, to sustain the weary with a word. He awakens Me morning by morning; He awakens My ear to listen as a disciple.
The Lord GOD has opened My ears, and I have not been rebellious, nor have I turned back.
I offered My back to those who struck Me, and My cheeks to those who tore out My beard. I did not hide My face from scorn and spittle.
Because the Lord GOD helps Me, I have not been disgraced; therefore I have set My face like {{chalamish|flint}}, and I know that I will not be put to shame.
The One who vindicates Me is near. Who will dare to contend with Me? Let us confront each other! Who has a case against Me? Let him approach Me!
Surely the Lord GOD helps Me. Who is there to condemn Me? See, they will all wear out like a garment; the moths will devour them.

units.label: A call to trust, a warning to self-reliance
units.note: lean on God's name, not your own firebrands

verses.text: Who among you fears the LORD and obeys the voice of His Servant? Who among you walks in darkness and has no light? Let him trust in the name of the LORD; let him lean on his God.

Behold, all you who kindle a fire, who array yourselves with firebrands, walk in the light of your fire and of the firebrands you have lit! This is what you will receive from My hand: You will lie down in a place of torment.

gaal.gloss: To redeem, to act as kinsman-deliverer for one who cannot free themselves. God asks whether His hand is too short to redeem, a rhetorical denial; the failure is never His power, it is Israel's sin. The word anchors the whole Servant section, since it is the Servant who will accomplish the redemption Israel could not achieve for herself.

limmud.gloss: One taught, instructed, a disciple. The Servant is given the tongue of the taught, so that His speech to the weary flows from an ear that is opened morning by morning to listen. It pictures a life of daily, unhurried attentiveness to the Father before there is a word for anyone else.

chalamish.gloss: Flint, hard rock. To set the face like flint is to fix oneself with unmovable resolve toward a course already known to bring suffering. Luke uses the same picture in Greek when Jesus set His face to go to Jerusalem, Luke 9:51, deliberately walking toward the cross.

basic.context: This is the third of four Servant Songs in Isaiah, the poems that describe a mysterious figure who will accomplish God's rescue. Here Israel is told plainly that her exile is not God's failure or forgetfulness, she sold herself through sin. Against that backdrop stands the Servant, whose ear is open to God and who absorbs abuse without retaliating or running.
basic.hermeneutics: The chapter has two halves that interpret each other: Israel's self-inflicted judgment, and the Servant's innocent suffering. Israel deserved what happened to her; the Servant did not deserve what happens to Him, yet He accepts it anyway. That contrast, deserved suffering versus willing, undeserved suffering, is the theological engine that drives toward Isaiah 53.
basic.originalLanguages: God asks if His hand is too short to ga'al, redeem, His people, a flat no. The Servant is given the tongue of limmud, one taught, so He can sustain the weary with a word shaped by daily listening. And He sets His face like challamish, flint, immovable toward the suffering ahead. Every word points to a will that is settled, obedient, and unshaken.
basic.typology: The Servant's opened ear, struck back, and set face all foreshadow the passion of Christ, who was flogged, spat upon, and mocked, and who set His face to go to Jerusalem knowing what awaited Him there. His refusal to hide His face from shame anticipates Gethsemane and Golgotha.
basic.christ: The gospels describe Jesus struck, spat upon, and His beard reportedly plucked in mockery, matching verse 6 almost word for word, and Luke 9:51 echoes the flint-set face of verse 7. Jesus is the true Servant who listens perfectly to the Father and does not turn back, even to the cross, trusting the One who vindicates Him.
basic.god: God is not a forgetful or defeated deity; Israel's exile was just judgment for real sin, not evidence that His arm had grown short. Yet the same God who judges also raises up a Servant who absorbs judgment willingly, showing that His justice and His mercy are never in tension, they meet in the Servant.
basic.crossReferences: Luke 9:51 shows Jesus setting His face toward Jerusalem. Matthew 26:67 and 27:26 describe Him struck and spat upon. Luke 22:63-65 records the mockery. Romans 8:33-34 echoes the courtroom language of verse 8, who shall bring a charge against God's elect.
basic.oneStory: Where Israel's story is one of self-inflicted exile, the Servant's story is one of willing, undeserved suffering offered in trust. That obedient trust, carried all the way to the cross by Jesus, becomes the ground on which every other failed story can be forgiven and remade.

context.literary:
Isaiah 50 is built as three panels with a changing voice, and the changes of voice are the structure. In verses 1 to 3 the LORD speaks, in a courtroom style of rapid questions. In verses 4 to 9 an unnamed first person speaks, and it is not the LORD, because he refers to 'the Lord GOD' as the one who helps him. In verses 10 and 11 a third voice, which sounds like the prophet or the LORD commenting on the Servant, turns to the audience and asks who among them will listen. The reader has to work out who is speaking, and the answer is the point: the first person of verses 4 to 9 is the same Servant introduced in Isaiah 42:1 and 49:1.

The middle panel is held together by the sacred title 'the Lord GOD', which appears in verses 4, 5, 7 and 9, a refrain that frames every claim the Servant makes. Each time the claim is the same shape: He gave, He opened, He helps, He helps. The Servant never says what He has done for Himself. Alongside it runs a movement from the ear to the mouth to the back to the face. First He hears (verses 4 and 5), then He speaks (verse 4), then He is struck (verse 6), then He looks his enemies in the eye (verses 7 to 9). The body is surrendered part by part while the will stays whole.

The opening panel is a pair of unanswerable questions, a written document and a creditor, followed by a pair of unanswered ones, 'Why was no one there when I arrived?' The silence of verse 2 is not God's absence but Israel's. He came and no one answered. That silence is exactly what the second panel reverses, because a man now stands there who does answer, and whose ear is already open when the morning begins.

The chapter then closes with a fork. Verse 10 offers trust to those who walk in darkness, verse 11 promises torment to those who light their own fires. Isaiah regularly ends a section with two roads, and the same pair of choices will meet the reader again in chapters 55 and 66.
context.historical:
The first hearers were exiles in or near Babylon, probably in the decades before Cyrus the Persian took the city in 539 BC. They carried a nagging question. Had the LORD simply discarded them? Verse 1 draws on two pieces of daily life that every family understood. One is the written certificate of divorce, which Deuteronomy 24:1 describes as a document a husband writes, hands to his wife and uses to send her away. The other is debt slavery, in which a creditor could take a family's children to settle what was owed, as the widow fears in 2 Kings 4:1 and as the poor of Nehemiah's day suffered, Nehemiah 5:5. The LORD asks them to produce either paper. If He had divorced them, where is the certificate? If He had sold them to pay a debt, who is the creditor? There is no such person, because the LORD owes nothing to anyone. The sale was of their own making.

The tension with Jeremiah 3:8 is worth noticing. There God says of northern Israel, 'I gave her a certificate of divorce and sent her away.' Isaiah and Jeremiah are not contradicting one another. Jeremiah speaks of a real separation that sin had brought about; Isaiah insists that the LORD will not be pinned to a final, legal divorce, and that He has never handed His people over to someone else.

The violence in verse 6 would have been understood as the worst kind of humiliation. To pull out someone's beard was to treat a man as nothing, as David's envoys learned when the Ammonites shaved half their beards, 2 Samuel 10:4. Spitting was an ancient gesture of contempt. Lamentations 3:30 pictures the faithful sufferer offering his cheek to the one who would strike him, so the Servant's posture was not unknown in Israel's prayers. The surprise is that He chooses it, and that it is Israel's God who vindicates a man treated this way.

Fire in verse 11 has a clear background. Exiles were tempted by the lights of the surrounding culture, with its fires, lamps and astral religion. Isaiah has already mocked the craftsman who warms himself at the same wood from which he carves his god, Isaiah 44:14 to 20. The people who kindle their own fire for light are those who trust their own devices instead of the LORD.
context.canonical:
The Servant Songs belong together, and this is the third of four. Isaiah 42:1 to 4 introduced the Servant as gentle in manner and firm in purpose; Isaiah 49:1 to 6 let Him speak of His calling and of labouring in vain, with a vindication that remains with the LORD; this poem now tells of the price of obedience; Isaiah 52:13 to 53:12 will show where that price leads. Each Song deepens what the previous one began. 'My vindication is with the LORD' in 49:4 becomes 'The One who vindicates Me is near' in 50:8, and the sufferer who seems to labour in vain is declared right.

Within the Old Testament the Servant's opened ear gathers up other voices. Psalm 40:6 says 'my ears You have opened' and then speaks of delight in God's will, with the law within the heart. The word 'disciple' in verse 4 reappears when the LORD promises that Zion's children will all be taught, Isaiah 54:13, and Jesus quotes that very promise in John 6:45. The Servant, in other words, is the first and model disciple, and His people share in what He has.

In the New Testament the Gospels narrate the poem almost scene by scene. Jesus predicts that He will be mocked, insulted, spat upon and flogged, Luke 18:32 and 33, and Matthew 26:67 and Mark 14:65 show the spitting and the blows at the trial. Matthew 27:30 repeats it at the Praetorium. Luke 9:51 says Jesus 'resolutely set out for Jerusalem', which many hear as an echo of the flint-set face. Peter, who stood in the high priest's courtyard, later writes that 'He did not retaliate' and 'entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly', 1 Peter 2:23, language that reads like a summary of verses 6 to 9.

Paul's triumphant questions in Romans 8:33 and 34, 'Who will bring any charge against God's elect? ... Who is there to condemn us?', borrow the courtroom shape of verses 8 and 9, and then place the risen and interceding Christ where Isaiah placed the LORD who helps. The believer stands acquitted on the strength of the Servant's own acquittal.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Isaiah wanted the exiles to stop reading their circumstances as proof that God was weak or had changed His mind. The first panel is a gentle but firm correction. Their trouble came from what they had done, and the cure does not require a new cause. If the LORD has not divorced them and has no creditor, then the door is open the moment they turn around.

The Servant section is meant to give them someone to look at, not just something to understand. They are asked to see a person who hears first and speaks second, who is made to suffer for it and who does not reply with bitterness or with retreat. The prophet does not pretend that faithfulness is rewarded quickly. He shows that obedience can look like defeat for a time, and that God's verdict still arrives.

Then comes the pivot that the whole chapter has been aimed at, verse 10. 'Who among you fears the LORD and obeys the voice of His Servant?' The listeners are asked to take the Servant's side in the dispute. Anyone sitting in the dark of exile may lean on the LORD's name. Anyone preferring the comfort of his own light, whether a political scheme, a foreign alliance or a household god, is told what that light will produce. Isaiah's aim is a decision, made while the facts are still painful.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes what happened to the Servant and what Israel brought on herself; it does not tell believers to seek out abuse or to stay passively in harm. Verse 6 is a record of what this particular Servant did in His particular calling, and the Gospels show that He did it to carry out a task that only He could do. To turn it into a rule for anyone being mistreated, including those in abusive homes, would be to misuse it. Peter, who writes of this same pattern, is addressing slaves who suffer unjustly for doing right and is not praising suffering for its own sake, 1 Peter 2:19 to 21.

What does carry across is the posture behind the pain. Believers are told to fix their eyes on Jesus, who scorned the shame and endured the cross, Hebrews 12:2, and to follow His example by not retaliating, 1 Peter 2:23. The ear that listens each morning is also a pattern, because the Servant's strength to speak to the weary was drawn from time spent hearing. Verse 10 is a direct command: fear the LORD, obey the voice of His Servant, and lean on God in the dark. And verse 11 is a warning against self-made light, which is as relevant to a modern believer's anxious scheming as to an exile's.

debates.question: Who is the speaker in verses 4 to 9?

views.label: The Servant of the LORD, ultimately Jesus
views.case: The speaker is clearly the figure who appeared in Isaiah 42:1 and 49:1 to 6, with a mouth made ready by God and a mission that includes Israel itself. The Gospels narrate the beatings and the spitting that verse 6 describes, and verse 10 calls the speaker 'His Servant' directly. The Church has read the poem as the voice of Christ from the earliest centuries.

views.label: The prophet Isaiah himself
views.case: Some scholars hear the voice of a prophet who endures mockery for his message, as Jeremiah did. Prophets in Israel were struck, put in stocks and ridiculed, Jeremiah 20:2 and 20:7. On this view the chapter describes a suffering prophet whom God vindicates.

views.label: Faithful Israel, personified
views.case: Isaiah 49:3 names the Servant 'Israel', so some take the speaker as the faithful remnant or the nation at its best, suffering in exile and trusting God for deliverance.

debates.bearing: The surrounding Songs prevent the reading from becoming small. In 49:5 and 6 the Servant has a mission to Israel, which means He cannot be the whole of Israel, and in this poem He obeys perfectly where Israel has just been shown to rebel. Isaiah himself may be the first to speak of such a life, but the New Testament writers saw that no prophet matched the picture, and Jesus did.

debates.question: What is the fire of verse 11?

views.label: Self-made light, human schemes in place of God
views.case: The people who 'kindle a fire' and 'array yourselves with firebrands' stand in contrast to the one who walks in darkness and trusts the LORD. The fire is a light of their own making, such as political alliances, foreign religion or sheer self-reliance. The promised outcome, that they will 'lie down in a place of torment', answers the false light with real darkness.

views.label: The fire of judgment they ignite themselves
views.case: Others read the fire as the very instrument of their ruin. By trusting their own sparks they walk into the flames, an ironic reversal in which what they kindle becomes their punishment. This fits Isaiah's fondness for sins that backfire on the sinner.

debates.bearing: Both readings reject any claim that people can supply their own light, and both set the exile's darkness, which can be borne with trust, against the dazzle of a self-lit path, which cannot. Either way, the fork of verse 10 and verse 11 is the same: trust the LORD in the dark, or be consumed by a light you made.

study.originalLanguages:
The word for what the Servant is given in verse 4 is 'discipleship' in the BSB, and the Hebrew is a plural noun, literally the tongue of 'the taught ones'. The same plural turns up in Isaiah 8:16, 'among my disciples', and in 54:13, where the children of Zion are 'taught by the LORD'. So the Servant is not a solitary genius. He belongs to a whole company of the taught, and He is the pattern of what the rest are to become. The verb 'awakens' in verse 4 comes from the root that also gives the cry 'Awake, awake' in 51:9 and 51:17. The Servant is the one who is awakened each dawn, and later the arm of the LORD and Jerusalem are summoned to wake in the same way.

Verse 1 uses two verbs about commerce. The LORD asks to whom He 'sold' them, and then says they 'were sold' for their iniquities. The sale is the Israelites' own, and the grammar shifts from an active question to a passive statement of fact, so that the guilty party is plain though not named. In 52:3 the LORD returns to the idea: 'You were sold for nothing, and without money you will be redeemed.' What was sold cheaply is bought back at no charge to the people. The 'iniquities' and 'transgressions' of verse 1 are the same pair that will return in 53:5 as the Servant is 'pierced for our transgressions' and 'crushed for our iniquities'. Here Israel is sold because of them; there the Servant is hurt because of them.

In verse 2 the question 'Is My hand too short?' uses a verb meaning to be short, cut off or fall short. The LORD asks it again in Numbers 11:23 about His arm, in the wilderness when Moses doubted that meat could be found for a whole people. The question is about power, and the answer both times is that His reach has never failed.

The two verbs 'rebellious' and 'turned back' in verse 5 describe the pattern of Israel's history. The first is the verb of defiance used again in Isaiah 1:20, 'resist and rebel', and the second means to withdraw or draw back. The Servant is defined by the absence of both. Verse 7 says He has 'set My face like flint', and Luke 9:51 renders the idea into Greek as setting the face toward Jerusalem.

In verse 8 the verb 'vindicates' is the verb of the courtroom, to declare righteous. It is a close kin of the verb Isaiah uses in 53:11, 'will justify many'. The Servant who is justified by God will become the one who justifies others. The word for 'condemn' in verse 9 is the opposite pole, to declare guilty, and Paul inherits both words in Romans 8:33 and 34.

typology.type: The open ear and the faithful disciple, Isaiah 50:4 and 5
typology.fulfillment: Israel's calling in the wilderness was to hear. 'Listen, O Israel' stood at the head of the law, Deuteronomy 6:4, and Israel did not. The Servant is the Israelite who does. Jesus fulfils the pattern by rising before dawn to pray, Mark 1:35, and by saying that He speaks exactly what the Father has taught Him, John 8:28. The escalation is that His hearing is not only a model but a source: the weary hear a word that was first received in prayer, Matthew 11:28. The type falls short only in that the Servant here is described as taught, whereas Jesus is the eternal Son, who as a man learned obedience, Hebrews 5:8.

typology.type: The blows to the back, cheeks and beard, Isaiah 50:6
typology.fulfillment: The Servant's body takes the strikes that were meant to humiliate. At the trial of Jesus they spat in His face and struck Him, Matthew 26:67, and after Pilate's verdict they did it again with a staff, Matthew 27:30. Mark 15:19 adds that they knelt in mock homage. The correspondence is in the bearing as much as the blows: He gives His back and does not hide His face. The escalation is that these acts were the front end of a death that dealt with the sins Israel had just been told she was sold for. The type falls short because Isaiah gives no hint here of the purpose of this suffering; only chapter 53 supplies that.

typology.type: The face set like flint, Isaiah 50:7
typology.fulfillment: Luke records that Jesus 'resolutely set out for Jerusalem', Luke 9:51, at the moment when the road leads towards rejection. He predicts what awaits Him there, Luke 18:31 to 33, and still walks on. The picture is of a will that does not wobble when its destination is known. The author of Hebrews describes the same steadiness as enduring the cross for the joy set before Him, Hebrews 12:2. The type reaches full strength in Gethsemane, where the flint-faced man still prays for the cup to pass and yet submits, Matthew 26:39. The type falls short because Isaiah's Servant is promised that He will not be put to shame, while Jesus had to pass through shame to get there.

typology.type: The vindicator who is near, Isaiah 50:8 and 9
typology.fulfillment: The Servant calls for any accuser to step forward, and none can. The pattern is a courtroom where the defendant is vindicated before the verdict is read. Jesus is raised, and the resurrection is the Father's public declaration of His righteousness, Romans 1:4 and 1 Timothy 3:16. Paul then extends the Servant's confidence to all who are in Him, in Romans 8:33 and 34: no one can lay a charge or condemn. The type falls short because the Servant faces a hostile crowd with the confidence of one who is innocent; His people stand with the confidence of the guilty who have been given His righteousness.

study.christ:
The poem leads to Christ by direct correspondence. The Gospel writers do not quote the verses of Isaiah 50 the way they quote other passages, but the details of the Passion line up with them with unusual closeness. Jesus Himself foretold being mocked, insulted, spat upon and flogged, Luke 18:32 and 33, and the accounts of His trial record the blows, the spitting and the mockery of the 'Prophesy!' game, Matthew 26:67 and 68, Mark 14:65, John 18:22. Isaiah's Servant is struck on cheek and face, so is Jesus. He is spat upon, so is Jesus. He answers with no retaliation, and Peter, who watched, recalls that Christ 'did not retaliate' and 'entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly', 1 Peter 2:23.

It leads to Christ by the shape of His inner life. The Servant's day begins with an ear awakened by God, and Jesus's days begin with withdrawal to pray, Mark 1:35. The Servant's speech is meant 'to sustain the weary with a word', and Jesus invites 'all you who are weary and burdened' and promises rest, Matthew 11:28. The officers who were sent to seize Him came back saying that no one ever spoke like this man, John 7:46. What He says comes from what He hears, and He says so: He speaks 'exactly what the Father has taught Me', John 8:28.

It leads to Christ by way of the courtroom language of verses 8 and 9. The Servant asks who will dare to contend with Him and answers that all His accusers will wear out like a garment. In the trial of Jesus the opposite seems to be the case, because the accusers prevail. The resurrection reverses it. The One who vindicates is near, and He vindicates in the most public way possible. Paul rests the believer on this when he asks who will bring a charge against God's elect, Romans 8:33 and 34, and he answers by pointing to Christ who died, was raised and is interceding.

The poem also supplies the background to the 'I' of verse 10, who invites the exiles to obey the voice of the Servant. The Servant is the one in whom the LORD's own authority is spoken. To obey His voice is to take the Servant's side, and that is why the Gospels press for a decision about Jesus in the same pattern: whoever hears His words and does them is like a wise builder, Matthew 7:24, while those who walk by their own light are shown the end of it.

The caution is that this poem does not yet say why the Servant suffers. Isaiah 50 shows His obedience and His vindication but not the substitution; that waits for chapter 53. A reader who turns every detail here into a statement about atonement runs ahead of the text. The better reading is to see here the character of the One who will carry out the work, a man whose will is already surrendered, so that the cross will be His own act as well as something done to Him.
study.god:
The chapter shows God first as the one who refuses the role of defendant. The questions of verses 1 and 2 are not defensive; they are the voice of one who knows He has done nothing wrong. He has no divorce certificate to show, no creditor to name, no shortness of reach to confess. The honesty of the question matters, because the exiles' complaint was a theological one: that the LORD had let them go. He answers by pointing to His record and to His readiness. 'Why was no one there when I arrived?' is the voice of a husband who came home and found the house empty.

He is also the Lord of creation, whose rebuke dries up the sea and whose power dresses the heavens in black, verses 2 and 3. The language recalls the exodus, when He dried up the sea for His people, and also the plague of darkness, but here it is a reminder that the one who now asks to be trusted holds all of nature in His hand. The Creator is not outmatched by Babylon.

The refrain 'the Lord GOD helps Me' shows a God who gives His own to the Servant. He gives the tongue, He opens the ear, He helps, and He stands near. This is the Father in relation to the Son in the way the New Testament will describe it, with a Son who does nothing on His own, John 8:28, and a Father who never leaves Him alone, John 16:32. The chapter holds in tension a God who permits His Servant to be struck and a God who is near to Him throughout. The hardest part of the text is that the helper and the one who allows the blows are the same. Isaiah does not explain it here; he only says that the Servant trusts it.

God is also the one who divides people by their answer to His Servant. Verse 10 and 11 are not threats thrown in at the end; they show that God takes the obedience of His Servant so seriously that to ignore His voice is to choose darkness. His holiness is not a mood but a settled response to those who prefer their own light.

For worship, the chapter teaches us to bring our sense of abandonment to a God who has already answered it. We are not asked to pretend that suffering is pleasant. We are asked to lean on the name of the LORD in the dark, as the Servant does, and to let the morning ear be opened before the day's voices begin.

crossReferences.note: The second Servant Song, which the third assumes. The Servant there speaks of being called from the womb and of labouring in vain, yet says that His vindication is with the LORD. Isaiah 50:4 to 9 shows how that vindication is held in the middle of mockery. Reading them together shows a Servant whose mission includes Israel but extends to the ends of the earth.

'You were sold for nothing, and without money you will be redeemed.' It picks up the sale of Isaiah 50:1 and answers it. The people sold themselves without receiving any payment, so the price of their redemption is not a price they can pay. Chapter 53 will show who pays it.

'He did not open His mouth.' The silence of the Servant before the people who strike Him in 50:6 becomes the silence of the lamb before the shearers. The two poems describe the same person, and the second shows what the first only implies, that the suffering is for others.

God says that He gave faithless Israel a certificate of divorce. The passage clarifies Isaiah 50:1: God does not deny that a separation occurred, but He denies that He sold His people to a creditor or that the separation is final. Both prophets agree that the cause lay with the people.

'Is the LORD's arm too short?' God's question to Moses in the wilderness is the same question He puts to Israel in Isaiah 50:2. The doubt about God's power in the exodus generation recurs in the exiles, and both times the LORD answers by pointing to what He has already done and will do.

'My ears You have opened' and 'I delight to do Your will.' The psalmist, like the Servant, has an opened ear and an inward law. Hebrews 10:5 to 10 takes this psalm as the voice of Christ coming into the world. Together they show that the Servant's open ear is the posture of the Son who has come to do God's will.

'All your sons will be taught by the LORD.' The Servant's 'tongue of the taught' in 50:4 turns out to be a seed from which the whole people grow. Those who obey His voice in 50:10 become the taught ones of chapter 54, and Jesus quotes this very verse in John 6:45.

The trial of Jesus before Caiaphas. They spit in His face, strike Him and slap Him, and mockingly tell Him to prophesy. The scene is a nearly point for point realization of Isaiah 50:6, though Matthew does not quote the verse. The Servant's body is given over to those who strike, and He does not retaliate.

'Jesus resolutely set out for Jerusalem.' The verb in Luke is a phrase about fixing the face on a goal, and it fits the flint-like face of Isaiah 50:7. Luke places it at the turning point of his Gospel, after which almost everything that Jesus does is on the road towards the cross.

Peter holds up Christ as an example to suffering servants. When they heaped abuse on Him, He did not retaliate, and He entrusted Himself to the One who judges justly. It reads as a summary of the Servant's refusal to turn back in Isaiah 50:5 to 9, with the added note that trust in God is what makes non-retaliation possible.

'Who will bring any charge against God's elect? ... Who is there to condemn us?' Paul turns Isaiah's courtroom challenge into the believer's own boast. The reason is that the one who was condemned has been raised and now intercedes. The Servant's vindication has become the church's.

Jesus 'endured the cross, scorning its shame.' The Servant who does not hide His face from scorn in Isaiah 50:6 is held up as the model of endurance for believers. The shame is real, and He scorns it, because of the joy set before Him and the vindication that is certain.

study.oneStory:
The chapter answers a question that the whole Bible keeps asking in different forms: can the covenant survive human failure? The first hearers asked it in Babylon. Adam and Eve asked it in the garden when they hid. Israel asked it at Sinai after the golden calf. Isaiah 50 answers that the bond is not broken by a legal document the LORD has never written, and not sold off to a creditor the LORD has never had. What is broken is the people's hearing, and the answer to a failure of hearing is someone who hears.

From the beginning of Genesis, God has spoken and creatures have been invited to listen. The serpent's first move was to cast doubt on what God had said, and Adam and Eve did not listen. Israel's long story is of prophets crying 'Listen!' and of ears that stayed shut, Isaiah 6:9 and 10. Against that background the Servant of this poem is the first person in Scripture to have an ear that stays open morning after morning. He does what Adam did not do, and He reverses the sequence of the fall by hearing, obeying and trusting where the first man doubted, listened to another voice and hid.

In the story the Bible tells, that obedience is not a private virtue but the foundation of a new humanity. Paul sets Adam's disobedience against Christ's obedience in Romans 5:19, and the author of Hebrews says that Jesus learned obedience through what He suffered, Hebrews 5:8. The obedience begun in the morning ear and carried to the flint-set face ends at the cross, which is where the debt that Israel was sold for is paid.

Isaiah 50 also sets up the rest of the story. It leads straight to Isaiah 52 and 53, where the silent sufferer is revealed as the one carrying the iniquities for which Israel was sold, and then to Isaiah 54, where the taught children appear. It leads outward to the early church, who are told to obey the voice of the Servant, and finally to the new creation, where the people of God no longer walk in the dark and no longer rely on their own fires. In Revelation 21:23 the city has no need of the sun or moon, because the glory of God gives it light. The light that Isaiah 50:11 refused to let people make for themselves is at last given to them, and the Lamb is its lamp.

quiz.q: According to Isaiah 50:1-3, why was Israel sent into exile?

options.text: Because of her own iniquities and transgressions, not because God's power or memory had failed.
options.note: Verse 1 states plainly that Israel was sold for her own sin.

options.text: Because God's hand had grown too short to redeem her.
options.note: Verse 2 explicitly denies this; God's power was never the problem.

options.text: Because God had permanently divorced her with no way back.
options.note: The chapter uses a divorce metaphor, but verse 1's rhetorical question shows no such certificate exists, so this overstates the case.

options.text: Because of a famine that God could not prevent.
options.note: The text names sin, not natural disaster, as the cause.

quiz.q: What marks the Servant's response to being struck and mocked in verses 5-6?

options.text: He does not rebel or turn back, and does not hide His face from scorn and spittle.
He calls down fire on His attackers.
options.note: The opposite; He submits rather than retaliates.

options.text: He flees before the abuse can happen.
options.note: He offers His back and cheeks; He does not flee.

options.text: He remains silent about God's help throughout.
options.note: He is largely silent under abuse, but He does speak of God's help vindicating Him.

quiz.q: What does it mean that the Servant 'set His face like flint'?

options.text: He fixed Himself with unmovable resolve to face the suffering ahead.
options.note: This is the meaning Luke 9:51 applies directly to Jesus going to Jerusalem.

options.text: His face literally turned to stone.
options.note: It is a figure of resolve, not a literal transformation.

options.text: He hardened His heart against God.
options.note: This inverts the image; His resolve is settled obedience toward God, not hardness against Him, though it correctly senses unbending resolve.

options.text: He refused to speak to anyone again.
options.note: The image is about resolve to endure suffering, not about silence toward people generally.

quiz.q: What is the closing call of verses 10-11 to those who fear the LORD but walk in darkness?

options.text: Trust in the name of the LORD and lean on God, rather than kindling your own firebrands.
options.note: Verse 10 calls for trust; verse 11 warns against self-made light that ends in torment.

options.text: Light your own fire so you are never without comfort.
options.note: Verse 11 warns this leads to a place of torment, not comfort.

options.text: Wait until the darkness lifts on its own before trusting God.
options.note: The call is to trust God precisely while still walking in darkness.

options.text: Obey the Servant's voice, since He alone can be fully trusted.
options.note: Close, and verse 10 does link fearing the LORD with obeying His Servant's voice, but the explicit command given is to trust and lean on God's name.

questions: Israel blamed God for her exile, but the text says she sold herself through sin. Where might you be tempted to blame God for consequences that are really the fruit of your own choices?
The Servant offered His back to those who struck Him rather than retaliating or hiding. Where is God asking you to absorb wrong rather than repay it, trusting Him to vindicate you?
The Servant set His face like flint toward suffering He knew was coming. What is one hard, right thing you are avoiding that requires that same settled resolve?

Verse 10 asks who among those in darkness will trust in the name of the LORD rather than lighting their own fire. What firebrands, plans, comforts, or self-reliance, are you tempted to kindle instead of trusting God?
Jesus is the Servant who listened perfectly where we do not. How does knowing His obedience, not yours, is what secures your redemption change the way you carry your own failures this week?

translationNotes.note: Certificate of divorce renders a specific legal formula; the rhetorical question assumes no such document exists, God has not formally cast Israel off.
Tongue of discipleship, limmudim, can also be rendered tongue of the learned or the taught; it emphasizes a speech shaped by daily instruction rather than natural eloquence.
Firebrands renders a term for sparks or burning arrows; the picture is of people who manufacture their own light and warmth apart from God, only to be consumed by the very fire they lit.
